name: Yusuf Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Yusuf, 43, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, repairing homes and wiring small businesses. I'm about the middle of the crew for skill; I can handle routine faults, and I call the lead electrician when the readings don't fit. My partner Kim works on a packing line, our children are twelve and fourteen, and we've a mortgage with barely two weeks of expenses saved; my pay is low and there are few similar electrical jobs nearby. I use AI daily to tidy anonymous job notes and suggest a parts checklist, then check everything against the real site; I enjoy a clean repair but hate having to chase next week's hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a useful checklist doesn't need to change the world to save a trip. We can keep the bits that work and forget the sales speech. I'd rather see the saved time in our day than another promise about what somebody might pay us later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about money before the big AI story starts. My wage and Kim's meet the mortgage and basics, but two weeks saved isn't much when either of us loses overtime. My daily tool doesn't create a second van or another employer round the corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd cancel the 14 monthly music subscription and put the saving toward the ordinary bills. In the first year I'd offer two evening paper-drawing study sessions a month through a free noticeboard, only for prepaid bookings and with no upfront spending or missed paid shifts. I'd keep the electrical shifts and daily checked notes; any tutorial money would be extra, not something I'd count before a booking existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a small idea I can try without borrowing. I like finding a practical next move. I don't like how many practical next moves it takes to cover one ordinary month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you offer in the study sessions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help vocational students read a simple circuit drawing on paper, not assess qualifications or tell anyone they're ready to wire a house. I'd charge 15 for a booked session and keep the exercise within what I can explain confidently. If no one booked, I'd spend nothing and keep doing my paid job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the sessions fit around the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kim and I would agree two evenings that didn't disrupt the children's school routine or our paid work. I wouldn't turn every night into another shift. A little extra income isn't worth a plan nobody in the house can live with.

I'd want **saved time** to appear in the working day rather than a distant pay promise.
think: Both wages cover basics, but **two weeks saved** leaves little protection against lost overtime.
My daily AI tool can't create **nearby employers** or spare equipment when money gets tight.

Offer two **prepaid tutorials** monthly at 15 each on evenings Kim agrees, without upfront spending or missed paid shifts.
Keep **electrical shifts** and checked daily notes, counting no tutorial income before bookings exist.
feel: **Anxious but inventive**, trying an affordable small idea without assuming customers or replacement wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the writing and ordering change before the hands-on jobs. Let's test the checklist against the actual van stock rather than cheer the screen. I don't mind learning early, but I want the time it takes included in the paid day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink if faster quoting makes the firm expect the same jobs with fewer electrician days. Kim's line work is mostly physical, so I don't expect thinking tools alone to remove that wage now. With our buffer so small, even a short run of fewer electrical shifts would make the mortgage difficult.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask to try the approved AI ordering tool during normal paid shifts, with no fee charged to me. Over the first year I'd compare twenty suggested parts lists with actual site needs and correct the errors before placing orders. I'd keep the music subscription cancelled and offer tutorials on two monthly evenings agreed with Kim around the children and our paid work, only prepaid and without upfront spending or missed paid shifts; free AI explanations could reduce demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and interested in whether I can avoid the wasted parts trip. I don't need to protect every old method. I do need my new method to leave a wage at the end of the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check a suggested order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd record which part was wrong and whether the drawing or the suggestion caused the problem. I'd check the actual specification before ordering, not ask the same tool to congratulate its own answer. A fast list is useful only when the part fits the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if nobody wanted the tutorials once free explanations improved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the day job and spend nothing chasing the missing bookings. The tutorials are a small possible extra, not our mortgage plan. I'd rather stop an experiment that doesn't earn than borrow to keep calling it a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work 2028 changes the thinking side, then capable robots reach physical jobs around 2031. I wouldn't sell the tutorials as a future-proof answer when AGI could explain the drawings too. I'd want an honest plan for paid hours before the robots were already ordered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a big share of my electrical hours to go when capable robots can do ordinary repairs. Kim's packing work could also change, so I can't count on one physical wage rescuing the other. Two weeks saved won't carry the mortgage through the gap I picture, and a clever tool doesn't soften that arithmetic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the subscription cancelled and take both wage records and the mortgage statement to free household advice. In 2029 I'd enrol in an evening building-controls course only with all fees funded and every basic paid shift retained. I'd keep earning in electrical work while checking actual vacancies and wouldn't include tutorial income in the post-AGI budget unless prepaid bookings really existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, with a head full of possible moves and not much cash behind them. I wake up doing the same mortgage sum. I can still ask for help and check a course, but I can't make two weeks of savings become a year by being enthusiastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the adviser to check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask which costs we could change, what support we could actually apply for and what a lender might discuss before a missed payment. I wouldn't count any payment or mortgage change until agreed. I need the adviser to show the holes in our plan, not just make me feel organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course funding did not appear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and ask about employer-funded alternatives, without saying I had enrolled. I wouldn't raid grocery money or lose basic shifts for the course. Building controls could face AGI and robots too, so I'd want actual work to test the skills against.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to test one small course without pretending study is a new wage. Thinking AGI comes in 2031 and capable robots around 2034. I'd use the warning to check actual paid options, not just get better at talking about adaptation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink, but with more time I don't regard the big loss as decided already. The mortgage still rests on two wages and very little spare cash. I'd need every step to work alongside the income we actually have, not a future job somebody says ought to exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd enrol in the evening controls course only with all fees funded and every basic paid shift retained. We'd keep the subscription cancelled and use free budget advice this year. During 2032 I'd apply for actual paid maintenance vacancies only on written pay and hours covering the mortgage and essentials, keeping current work until an acceptable offer existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more chance to check the route than in the two-year picture. I could discover a course wasn't useful before spending more time on it. I'd still have to put groceries on the table during that discovery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check a course against a maintenance vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the class included supervised testing of heating and lighting controls, then compare that practice with the systems named in a real vacancy. My present licence and ordinary repair experience don't make me competent on every control panel. I'd need the employer to explain further requirements and paid supervised learning, without counting a new qualification or wage before either existed. A new title isn't enough if the paid hours still miss the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the tutorial sideline continue in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue only when real prepaid bookings existed, with no upfront spending or missed paid shifts. I wouldn't count that sideline in a budget before the money was booked. If AGI removed the demand, I'd stop offering it rather than promise the family a wage from an empty noticeboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years lets us make a plan with room to change our minds. I'd keep testing useful tools, but I'd measure preparation by real wages and manageable costs. Nobody pays our mortgage in certificates or clever answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and still need earnings when robots follow around 2039. A decade makes the machine question less urgent, but it doesn't change our low pay or two-week reserve now. A vehicle repair or lost shifts would still put the household under pressure long before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the music subscription cancelled and use free budget advice now. I'd enrol in the evening controls course only with full fees funded and every basic paid shift retained, reviewing actual wages and vacancies each year before any further study. In 2037 I'd accept actual paid maintenance work only with written pay and hours covering the mortgage and essentials, keeping present work without an acceptable offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about current money, with room to think more calmly about the later machines. I can still enjoy trying a tool without asking it to save the house. The longer warning should let me be a father as well as somebody preparing for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the annual review measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kim and I would look at the actual paid hours from both jobs, the mortgage and essential spending. If wages weakened sooner, we'd bring advice and applications forward. A ten-year warning isn't an instruction to wait while today's account runs down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about their own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to check the next real course choice and ask what they liked doing, without pretending I knew the safe answer for 2039. I'd show them that I still ask for help on difficult faults. Being willing to learn matters, but it doesn't make every learning promise affordable or true.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect large electrical-hour losses once capable robots follow around 2031, and our reserve is so short. Fully funded study preserving every basic paid shift, early hours notice and advice based on real household numbers would help. I can learn a tool quickly; I can't earn the mortgage twice in the same hour.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether trying lots of small ideas gets tiring. It does, especially when an experiment has to justify itself before the next bill. I like being curious, but I'd also like one month when curiosity wasn't doing a second job as emergency planning.

headlineQuote: I can learn a tool quickly; I can't earn the mortgage twice in the same hour.
portrait: At **43**, Yusuf is an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and licence, low pay, and about two weeks of expenses saved.
He and **Kim**, his packing-line partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with few nearby electrical alternatives.
He uses **AI daily** for checked notes and parts ideas, while asking the lead electrician about faults beyond his ordinary competence.
His **small experiments** never become guaranteed income; faster change leaves him alarmed, and longer warnings still preserve present household money worries.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before expected large hour losses when capable robots follow around 2031, with almost no reserve.
whatWouldHelp: **Fully funded study** must preserve every basic paid shift, alongside early hours notice and advice grounded in actual household figures.
